stem: An online retailer's traffic triples during holiday sales and drops back to normal in January. On premises, it bought enough servers for the peak, and most of them sit idle for ten months a year.
prompt: Which benefit of the AWS Cloud addresses this problem MOST directly?

options.text: Lower latency through a content delivery network
options.why: A CDN speeds up content delivery, but it does not change how much server capacity the retailer owns.

options.text: Built-in compliance with every industry standard
options.why: AWS supports many compliance programs, but compliance has nothing to do with idle capacity.

options.text: Elasticity to add and remove capacity with demand
options.why: Elasticity lets the retailer scale out for the holiday peak and scale back in afterwards, paying only for what it uses.

options.text: Global reach through Regions around the world
options.why: More locations help with latency for distant users, but they do not stop capacity from sitting idle after the peak.

explanation.answer: Elasticity means capacity grows and shrinks automatically or on demand. Instead of buying for the peak, the retailer runs what it needs each day.
explanation.concept: The six advantages of cloud computing include trading fixed expense for variable expense and no longer guessing capacity. Elasticity is how you stop guessing.
explanation.examTip: Spiky or seasonal demand + idle hardware = elasticity (stop guessing capacity).

stem: A product team used to wait six weeks for new servers to be ordered, racked and configured. On AWS, the team can launch test environments in minutes and delete them when the experiment ends.
prompt: Which cloud benefit does this describe?

options.text: Data sovereignty
options.why: Data sovereignty is about where data is stored and which laws apply, not provisioning speed.

options.text: High availability
options.why: High availability keeps workloads running through failures; it does not describe faster provisioning.

options.text: Economies of scale
options.why: Economies of scale lower prices because AWS buys at huge volume; they are not about how quickly a team can experiment.

options.text: Increased speed and agility
options.why: Getting resources in minutes instead of weeks lets teams experiment more often at lower cost, which is agility.

explanation.answer: Agility is the ability to get resources quickly, try ideas and throw them away cheaply. It shortens the time from idea to result.
explanation.concept: Speed and agility come from on-demand, self-service provisioning. When experiments are cheap, teams can innovate faster.
explanation.examTip: Minutes instead of weeks to get resources = speed and agility.

stem: A startup's finance lead wants to avoid large upfront hardware purchases and instead pay monthly for the IT resources the company actually consumes.
prompt: Which statement BEST describes this change?

options.text: Moving from capital expense to variable expense
options.why: Paying as you go replaces large upfront capital purchases with ongoing variable costs tied to usage.

options.text: Moving from operational to capital expenditure
options.why: Cloud spending is generally operational; the startup is moving away from capital expenditure, not toward it.

options.text: Moving from usage pricing to fixed contracts
options.why: Fixed contracts are the opposite of paying for actual consumption.

options.text: Moving from variable expense to capital expense
options.why: This is the reverse: buying hardware upfront is a capital expense, which the startup wants to avoid.

explanation.answer: With the cloud, you trade capital expense (data centers, servers bought upfront) for variable expense, paying only for what you consume.
explanation.concept: Capital expenditure (CapEx) is money spent upfront on assets. Operational or variable expenditure (OpEx) is paid as you use resources.
explanation.examTip: Avoid upfront hardware purchases = trade CapEx for variable OpEx.

stem: A company notices that AWS has lowered prices for several services many times over the years, even though the company's own data center costs keep rising.
prompt: Which cloud advantage explains why AWS can keep lowering prices?

options.text: Go global in minutes
options.why: Global reach is about deploying in many locations quickly, not about price reductions.

options.text: Benefit from massive economies of scale
options.why: Because AWS aggregates usage from hundreds of thousands of customers, it achieves lower costs and passes savings on.

options.text: Stop guessing capacity
options.why: Not guessing capacity avoids idle resources for the customer, but it does not explain AWS price cuts.

options.text: Stop spending money on data centers
options.why: This helps the customer avoid facility costs, but it does not explain why AWS prices fall over time.

explanation.answer: Economies of scale let AWS buy and operate infrastructure more cheaply than any single company could, which results in lower pay-as-you-go prices.
explanation.concept: Aggregated demand across many customers lowers the per-unit cost of compute, storage and networking.
explanation.examTip: Lower prices because AWS is huge = economies of scale.

stem: A gaming company based in Canada wants to launch servers close to new players in Japan and Brazil next month without building any data centers there.
prompt: Which benefit of the AWS Cloud makes this possible?

options.text: Automatic compliance certification
options.why: Compliance programs do not place servers near players.

options.text: Unlimited free data transfer
options.why: Data transfer out of AWS is generally charged, and it has nothing to do with server location.

options.text: Going global in minutes with AWS Regions
options.why: The company can deploy in Regions near Japan and Brazil in minutes, giving players lower latency.

options.text: Pay-as-you-go pricing
options.why: Pricing affects cost, but it does not provide infrastructure in distant countries.

explanation.answer: AWS Regions around the world let you deploy applications close to users with a few clicks, reducing latency without building facilities.
explanation.concept: Going global in minutes is one of the six advantages of cloud computing.
explanation.examTip: Reach new countries fast without building data centers = global infrastructure (go global in minutes).

stem: A company is comparing the cost of staying in its own data center with moving to AWS. The CFO asks which costs should be included to make a fair comparison.
prompt: Which cost is MOST often overlooked when calculating the on-premises side?

options.text: The cost of AWS Support plans
options.why: Support plans are an AWS cost, not an on-premises one.

options.text: The hourly price of Amazon EC2 instances
options.why: EC2 pricing belongs on the AWS side of the comparison, not the on-premises side.

options.text: The license fee for the AWS Management Console
options.why: The AWS Management Console has no license fee.

options.text: Power, cooling, space and staff to run the hardware
options.why: A fair total cost of ownership includes facilities, power, cooling and labor, not only server prices.

explanation.answer: Total cost of ownership (TCO) compares the full cost of each option. On premises, that includes facilities, power, cooling, hardware refreshes and the people who run them.
explanation.concept: TCO analysis looks beyond the purchase price to every direct and indirect cost of running IT.
explanation.examTip: TCO = include facilities, power, cooling, staff and refresh cycles, not just hardware.

stem: A bank keeps its core banking system in its own data center for regulatory reasons but runs its mobile app back end on AWS. The two environments are connected.
prompt: Which cloud deployment model is the bank using?

options.text: Hybrid
options.why: Hybrid deployments connect on-premises infrastructure with cloud resources, as the bank does.

options.text: Multi-Region
options.why: Multi-Region describes using several AWS Regions, not combining a data center with the cloud.

options.text: On-premises (private cloud)
options.why: A purely on-premises model would not run the mobile back end on AWS.

options.text: Cloud (all-in)
options.why: An all-in cloud deployment runs every part of the application in the cloud, which is not the case here.

explanation.answer: A hybrid deployment links cloud resources with existing on-premises infrastructure, often because some systems must stay on premises.
explanation.concept: The three common deployment models are cloud (cloud-native), hybrid and on-premises (private cloud).
explanation.examTip: Some in the data center + some on AWS, connected = hybrid.

stem: A new startup builds its entire application on AWS from day one, using managed databases, serverless functions and object storage. It owns no servers.
prompt: Which deployment model does this describe?

options.text: On-premises
options.why: On-premises means running the application in your own data center.

options.text: Cloud (cloud-native)
options.why: Running every part of the application in the cloud from the start is the cloud, or cloud-native, deployment model.

options.text: Hybrid
options.why: Hybrid requires some on-premises infrastructure connected to the cloud; the startup has none.

options.text: Private cloud
options.why: A private cloud uses virtualization in your own data center, not AWS.

explanation.answer: A cloud-based (all-in) deployment runs all parts of the application in the cloud, either built natively or migrated.
explanation.concept: Cloud-native applications are designed to use managed services from the start.
explanation.examTip: Everything on AWS, nothing on premises = cloud deployment model.

stem: A company runs its own database servers and spends many engineering hours each month on patching, backups and hardware failures. Leadership wants engineers to spend that time on new features.
prompt: Which cloud advantage BEST addresses this goal?

options.text: Trade variable expense for capital expense
options.why: This reverses the real advantage, and it does not free engineers from database chores.

options.text: Increase the number of Availability Zones used
options.why: More AZs improve resilience, but engineers would still be doing the same maintenance work.

options.text: Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers
options.why: Managed services let AWS handle undifferentiated heavy lifting so teams focus on customers.

options.text: Buy larger servers to reduce the number to patch
options.why: Fewer, larger servers still need patching and backups by the company.

explanation.answer: Managed services such as Amazon RDS take over patching, backups and hardware management. This removes undifferentiated heavy lifting.
explanation.concept: Focusing on projects that differentiate the business, not racking and maintaining infrastructure, is a core cloud advantage.
explanation.examTip: Engineers stuck on patching and hardware = move to managed services (stop running data centers).

stem: A company's web application must keep running even if an entire data center loses power.
prompt: Which approach on AWS BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Store backups in the same Availability Zone
options.why: Backups in the same location are lost with it and do not keep the app running.

options.text: Use a larger Amazon EBS volume
options.why: Volume size does not protect against a data center outage.

options.text: Run the application on one large EC2 instance
options.why: A single instance in one location fails if that location fails.

options.text: Deploy across multiple Availability Zones
options.why: AZs are separate data centers with independent power, so the app keeps running if one fails.

explanation.answer: Availability Zones are physically separate groups of data centers in a Region. Spreading an application across AZs keeps it available when one AZ fails.
explanation.concept: High availability on AWS starts with removing single points of failure, such as running in only one AZ.
explanation.examTip: Survive a data center failure = multiple Availability Zones.

stem: A research lab needs 500 servers for a three-day simulation once a quarter and nothing in between.
prompt: Which AWS pricing characteristic makes the cloud a good fit?

options.text: Pay only for the resources used, when used
options.why: Pay-as-you-go pricing charges for the three days of use and nothing in between.

options.text: Long-term hardware leases
options.why: Leases still charge for servers when the lab is not using them.

options.text: Fixed monthly fees for each AWS account
options.why: AWS accounts do not have a fixed monthly fee for compute capacity.

options.text: Discounts for buying hardware upfront
options.why: AWS customers do not buy hardware upfront; that is the on-premises model.

explanation.answer: Pay-as-you-go pricing lets the lab run 500 servers for three days and stop paying when the simulation ends.
explanation.concept: On AWS you pay for what you use, without long-term contracts unless you choose them for a discount.
explanation.examTip: Short bursts of heavy use = pay-as-you-go.

stem: After moving to AWS, a company finds that many EC2 instances run at under 10% CPU all month.
prompt: Which practice would reduce cost while keeping the same performance?

options.text: Add more instances behind a load balancer
options.why: Adding instances increases cost when existing ones are already underused.

options.text: Rightsize to smaller instance types
options.why: Matching instance size to actual usage cuts cost without hurting performance.

options.text: Buy Reserved Instances for the current sizes
options.why: Committing to oversized instances locks in waste for one or three years.

options.text: Move the instances to a different Region
options.why: Changing Region does not fix oversized instances and can add data transfer costs.

explanation.answer: Rightsizing matches instance types and sizes to workload needs. Very low utilization is a sign that a smaller instance would do.
explanation.concept: Rightsizing is a continuous process; tools such as AWS Compute Optimizer recommend better-fitting sizes.
explanation.examTip: Low utilization = rightsize first, then commit to discounts.

stem: A company already owns Microsoft Windows Server licenses and wants to use them on AWS instead of paying for license-included instances.
prompt: What is this licensing approach called?

options.text: Pay-per-request licensing
options.why: Pay-per-request is a pricing model for some serverless services, not a way to reuse licenses.

options.text: License-included pricing
options.why: License-included pricing bundles the license cost into the instance price, the opposite of what the company wants.

options.text: Bring your own license (BYOL)
options.why: BYOL lets the company apply licenses it already owns, subject to the vendor's terms.

options.text: Savings Plans licensing
options.why: Savings Plans are compute discounts for a usage commitment; they are not a licensing approach.

explanation.answer: Bring your own license (BYOL) lets customers use existing software licenses on AWS. Some licenses require Dedicated Hosts to comply with vendor rules.
explanation.concept: Licensing is part of cloud economics: compare license-included options with BYOL when estimating cost.
explanation.examTip: Reuse licenses you already own = BYOL (sometimes needs Dedicated Hosts).

stem: A company moves its applications to AWS. Its operations team no longer replaces failed disks or schedules hardware refreshes.
prompt: How does this change MOST affect the company's costs?

options.text: It has little effect, because hardware work was cheap
options.why: Staff time on hardware is a real cost that goes away after migration.

options.text: It increases costs because AWS charges for hardware replacement
options.why: AWS does not bill customers separately for replacing failed hardware.

options.text: It removes all operations staff costs permanently
options.why: Staff are still needed to run, secure and optimize workloads on AWS; their focus changes.

options.text: It shifts staff time from hardware tasks to higher-value work
options.why: AWS handles physical infrastructure, so people can work on automation, security and new features.

explanation.answer: Moving to AWS removes hardware tasks from the customer's workload. The savings show up as staff time that can go to work that differentiates the business.
explanation.concept: Cloud economics includes labor costs. Operational savings come from not managing physical infrastructure.
explanation.examTip: Fewer hardware chores = staff move to higher-value work (not zero staff).

stem: A manager asks for a one-sentence definition of cloud computing.
prompt: Which definition is MOST accurate?

options.text: On-demand IT resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing
options.why: This is how AWS defines cloud computing: on-demand delivery of IT resources with pay-as-you-go pricing.

options.text: Buying software licenses that run without servers
options.why: Software licensing is not the same as delivering compute, storage and other IT resources.

options.text: Running virtual machines in your own data center
options.why: That is virtualization on premises, sometimes called a private cloud, not cloud computing from a provider.

options.text: Renting physical servers in a shared colocation facility
options.why: Colocation still means buying and managing your own hardware in someone else's building.

explanation.answer: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute, storage, databases and other IT resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing.
explanation.concept: You access technology services as needed from a provider instead of buying and maintaining data centers.
explanation.examTip: Cloud computing = on-demand + over the internet + pay-as-you-go.

stem: An architect explains that one application can handle growth by adding more servers over time, while another automatically shrinks to two servers every night.
prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes scalability from elasticity?

options.text: Scalability only shrinks resources; elasticity only grows them
options.why: Neither term is limited to one direction in that way.

options.text: Scalability handles growth; elasticity matches capacity to demand both ways
options.why: Scalability is the ability to grow, and elasticity automatically adds and removes capacity as demand changes.

options.text: They mean the same thing and can be used interchangeably
options.why: They are related but not identical; elasticity adds automatic scaling in both directions.

options.text: Scalability is for storage; elasticity is only for compute
options.why: Both ideas apply across compute, storage and databases.

explanation.answer: Scalability means a system can grow to handle more load. Elasticity means capacity automatically scales out and back in as demand rises and falls.
explanation.concept: Elastic systems avoid paying for idle resources during quiet periods.
explanation.examTip: Grows with load = scalable. Grows and shrinks automatically = elastic.

references.title: What is Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling?

stem: A company virtualizes servers in its own data center and gives internal teams a self-service portal to request virtual machines. No public cloud is involved.
prompt: Which deployment model does this describe?

options.text: Multi-account AWS deployment
options.why: Multi-account setups organize AWS accounts and require AWS.

options.text: Hybrid cloud
options.why: Hybrid requires a connection between on-premises resources and a cloud provider.

options.text: On-premises (private cloud)
options.why: Self-service virtualization inside your own data center is an on-premises, or private cloud, deployment.

options.text: Cloud-native deployment
options.why: Cloud-native applications run on a cloud provider such as AWS, not in a company data center.

explanation.answer: Deploying resources on premises with virtualization and resource management tools is sometimes called a private cloud.
explanation.concept: Private cloud gives some cloud-like self-service, but the company still buys and runs all the hardware.
explanation.examTip: Own data center + virtualization + no provider = on-premises (private cloud).

stem: A media company's video processing costs on AWS rise in months with many new uploads and fall in quiet months.
prompt: Which statement BEST explains this cost pattern?

options.text: The company is paying for peak capacity all year
options.why: Paying for peak all year would produce flat costs, not costs that follow usage.

options.text: The company signed a three-year Reserved Instance term
options.why: Reserved Instances produce steady committed costs, not costs that move with uploads.

options.text: AWS changes its prices every month based on demand
options.why: AWS does not reprice services monthly based on a single customer's demand.

options.text: Costs are variable and follow actual usage
options.why: With pay-as-you-go pricing, more processing in busy months means higher costs, and less in quiet months means lower costs.

explanation.answer: Variable expense means the bill tracks consumption. Busy months cost more and quiet months cost less.
explanation.concept: Variable costs remove the need to pay for capacity that sits idle in slow periods.
explanation.examTip: Bill rises and falls with usage = variable expense.

stem: Before migrating 400 servers, a company wants a data-driven business case that estimates its AWS costs from the actual utilization of its on-premises servers.
prompt: Which AWS offering is designed for this?

options.text: Migration Evaluator
options.why: Migration Evaluator collects on-premises utilization data and produces a business case with projected AWS costs.

options.text: AWS Application Migration Service
options.why: This service performs the actual rehost migration; it does not build the business case.

options.text: AWS Trusted Advisor
options.why: Trusted Advisor checks resources already running on AWS, not on-premises servers.

options.text: Amazon Inspector
options.why: Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities; it does not estimate migration costs.

explanation.answer: Migration Evaluator builds a data-driven business case for migrating to AWS by analyzing on-premises resource usage.
explanation.concept: Business cases for migration compare current costs with projected AWS costs based on real utilization, not guesses.
explanation.examTip: Business case before migrating = Migration Evaluator. Actually move servers = Application Migration Service.

stem: Before moving to AWS, a company often bought too many servers for a new product, or too few and had outages at launch.
prompt: Which cloud advantage helps the MOST with this problem?

options.text: Go global in minutes
options.why: Global reach helps with latency for distant users, not with estimating capacity.

options.text: Stop guessing capacity
options.why: You can start small and scale up or down as real demand appears, so you don't need to guess in advance.

options.text: Benefit from economies of scale
options.why: Economies of scale lower prices but do not solve over- or under-buying.

options.text: Trade variable expense for capital expense
options.why: This reverses the real advantage, which trades capital expense for variable expense.

explanation.answer: With the cloud you can access as much or as little capacity as you need and adjust within minutes, so capacity guessing goes away.
explanation.concept: Over-provisioning wastes money; under-provisioning hurts customers. The cloud removes the need to choose in advance.
explanation.examTip: Bought too many or too few servers = stop guessing capacity.

stem: A company wants backups and replicas of its data stored far apart so a natural disaster in one city cannot destroy every copy.
prompt: Which feature of AWS global infrastructure supports this?

options.text: Larger instance types with more memory
options.why: Instance size has nothing to do with protecting data from disasters.

options.text: A single Availability Zone with extra volumes
options.why: Everything in one AZ can be lost in the same event.

options.text: Multiple AWS Regions in separate geographies
options.why: Regions are geographically separate, so copies in two Regions survive a regional disaster.

options.text: Edge locations that cache content
options.why: Edge locations cache content for delivery; they are not where you keep disaster recovery copies.

explanation.answer: AWS Regions are separate geographic areas. Replicating data to a second Region protects against disasters that affect a whole area.
explanation.concept: Use multiple AZs for high availability, and multiple Regions for disaster recovery against large-scale events.
explanation.examTip: Protect against a city-wide disaster = copies in another Region.

stem: A CFO asks which cost would go away after moving every workload from the company's own data center to AWS.
prompt: Which cost is eliminated?

options.text: Paying for data transfer to the internet
options.why: Data transfer out to the internet is still charged on AWS.

options.text: Paying staff to manage applications
options.why: Staff still manage applications, data and security configurations on AWS.

options.text: Paying for compute capacity
options.why: The company still pays for compute on AWS, though on a usage basis.

options.text: Buying and refreshing physical servers
options.why: AWS owns and refreshes the physical hardware, so the company no longer buys servers.

explanation.answer: After migrating, the company stops buying, maintaining and refreshing physical hardware, because AWS owns the infrastructure.
explanation.concept: Moving to AWS changes costs from hardware ownership to usage-based service charges.
explanation.examTip: Gone after migration: hardware purchases and refreshes. Still there: usage charges and your team's work.

stem: A company wants to try a machine learning idea. If the idea fails, it wants to stop paying immediately.
prompt: Which characteristic of the cloud supports this kind of experimentation?

options.text: Low cost of failure with on-demand resources
options.why: Resources can be shut down at any time, so failed experiments stop costing money right away.

options.text: Fixed annual capacity reservations
options.why: Reservations charge for capacity whether or not the experiment continues.

options.text: Owning hardware that can be resold
options.why: Reselling hardware is slow and recovers only part of the cost.

options.text: Long-term commitments with discounts
options.why: Commitments reduce prices but keep you paying after an experiment ends.

explanation.answer: On-demand resources make failure cheap: you launch what you need, test the idea and shut it down if it doesn't work.
explanation.concept: Agility includes a lower cost of experimentation, which encourages innovation.
explanation.examTip: Try fast, fail cheap, stop paying = on-demand agility.

stem: A student says: "AWS is cheaper only because customers share physical servers with no isolation."
prompt: Which response is MOST accurate?

options.text: Correct; that is why AWS cannot be used for regulated data
options.why: AWS supports many regulated workloads under compliance programs such as PCI DSS and HIPAA.

options.text: Incorrect; lower costs come mainly from economies of scale
options.why: AWS's scale lowers per-unit costs, and customer workloads stay isolated from each other.

options.text: Incorrect; AWS is cheaper only because it has no staff costs
options.why: AWS has large staff costs; scale spreads them across many customers.

options.text: Correct; all AWS resources run on shared hardware with no isolation
options.why: AWS isolates customers through virtualization and offers dedicated options when needed.

explanation.answer: AWS lowers prices through economies of scale. Customer workloads are logically isolated, and Dedicated Instances or Dedicated Hosts provide physical isolation when required.
explanation.concept: Shared infrastructure with strong isolation is how cloud providers achieve scale securely.
explanation.examTip: Cheaper because of scale, not because of weak isolation.

stem: A company is building the business case for moving to AWS.
prompt: Which TWO are benefits of the AWS Cloud? (Select TWO.)

options.text: AWS manages your data classification for you
options.why: Classifying and protecting your data is your responsibility under the shared responsibility model.

options.text: Deploy worldwide in minutes
options.why: AWS Regions around the world let you reach new markets quickly.

options.text: No need to secure your applications
options.why: Customers remain responsible for securing their applications and data.

options.text: Software licenses are included at no extra cost
options.why: Many licenses cost extra or require bring your own license.

options.text: Trade fixed upfront costs for variable costs
options.why: Paying for what you use instead of buying hardware upfront is a core cloud benefit.

explanation.answer: Two of the six advantages of cloud computing are trading capital expense for variable expense, and going global in minutes.
explanation.concept: The six advantages: variable expense, economies of scale, stop guessing capacity, speed and agility, stop running data centers, go global in minutes.
explanation.examTip: Memorize the six advantages; watch for distractors that shift your security duties to AWS.
